sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Generics (introduced in Go 1.18) are now a standard part of the language and appear in the standard library's slices, maps, and cmp packages. Interviewers at companies that have upgraded to 1.18+ will ask about type parameters to see whether you understand the motivation, the constraints model, and the tradeoffs versus interface-based approaches. Understanding when generics help — and when they add accidental complexity — is the sign of an experienced Go engineer.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: A type parameter is a placeholder resolved at compile time, written in square brackets: func Map[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U. Constraints are interfaces that restrict which types can fill a type parameter — any means no restriction, comparable means the type supports == and !=, and you can define custom constraints using union elements (int | float64). The compiler generates or shares code for each concrete type instantiation depending on the implementation strategy (GC shapes). Type inference lets the compiler deduce type arguments from function arguments, so you rarely need to write them explicitly.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
• Type parameters: declared in [T constraint] before the function or type parameter list.
• any constraint: alias for interface{}; allows any type but no operations beyond assignment.
• comparable: allows == and !=; required for map keys and sets.
• cmp.Ordered: union constraint covering all integer, float, and string types; enables < > comparisons.
• Type inference: compiler deduces T from call-site arguments in most cases — no angle-bracket ceremony.
• Generics vs interfaces: use generics when you need to preserve concrete type information or avoid boxing; use interfaces when behaviour (method set) is the contract.
• When not to use generics: small one-off functions, when reflection or any is genuinely needed, or when constraints become more complex than the code they replace.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
• 'Why did Go add generics so late? What was the tradeoff?' — simplicity vs expressiveness; the team resisted until a clean design was found.
• 'What is the difference between any and comparable as constraints?' — comparable adds == support; any does not.
• 'Write a generic Min function.' — func Min[T cmp.Ordered](a, b T) T { if a < b { return a }; return b }
• 'When would you prefer an interface parameter over a type parameter?' — when you want runtime polymorphism, multiple concrete types in one collection, or the function is already simple.
• 'Can you use generics with methods?' — type parameters on methods are not yet allowed; only on types or package-level functions.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "Before generics, any reusable container or algorithm in Go required either code generation or interface{} with type assertions, both of which have real costs. Generics let me write a single Map or Filter function that works on any slice type while preserving compile-time type safety. The key concept I lean on is constraints: I use any when the function only needs to store or forward a value, comparable when I need a map key or equality check, and cmp.Ordered when I need less-than comparisons. I'm also deliberate about when not to use generics — if the constraint logic becomes harder to read than the code it's abstracting, I'll reach for a concrete type or an interface instead."
